title: Canonical Serre presentation for a prescribed rational pinning
statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple rational Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra], [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], and $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ a maximal abelian subalgebra acting diagonally over $\mathbf Q$. Suppose its root decomposition is $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in R}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, with $R\subset\mathfrak h^\vee\setminus\{0\}$ a reduced crystallographic root system and $\mathfrak g_\alpha=\{z:[h,z]=\alpha(h)z\text{ for every }h\in\mathfrak h\}$ one-dimensional. For each root let $h_\alpha$ be the element of $[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}]\subseteq\mathfrak h$ normalized by $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$. Fix a base $\Delta=\{\alpha_i:i\in I\}\subseteq R$, where $I$ is finite, such that the $\alpha_i$ are a basis of $\mathfrak h^\vee$ and every root has integral coordinates all of one sign. Choose nonzero $e_i\in\mathfrak g_{\alpha_i}$ and $f_i\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha_i}$ with $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$, and put $a_{ij}=\alpha_j(h_{\alpha_i})\in\mathbf Z$; thus $a_{ii}=2$ and $a_{ij}\leq0$ for $i\ne j$. Let $\mathfrak s(A)$ be the free rational Lie algebra on symbols $H_i,E_i,F_i$, modulo the Lie ideal generated by
$$[H_i,H_j],\quad [E_i,F_j]-\delta_{ij}H_i,\quad [H_i,E_j]-a_{ij}E_j,\quad [H_i,F_j]+a_{ij}F_j,$$
and by $(\operatorname{ad}E_i)^{1-a_{ij}}E_j$, $(\operatorname{ad}F_i)^{1-a_{ij}}F_j$ for $i\ne j$. Here free means that every assignment of the symbols to a rational Lie algebra extends uniquely to a rational Lie homomorphism, and $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. The assignment $H_i\mapsto h_{\alpha_i}$, $E_i\mapsto e_i$, $F_i\mapsto f_i$ induces a rational Lie algebra isomorphism $\phi:\mathfrak s(A)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathfrak g$. The empty base is included.

source.place: Section 23h, Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503--504; characteristic-zero extension and normalized simple-root triples on p.508. The comparison with an arbitrary prescribed rational pinning is an agent-stated supporting lemma, not a quotation of the printed existence theorem. The letter typos on p.504 are read as [X_i,Y_i]=H_i, [H_i,Y_j]=-n(i,j)Y_j, and (ad Y_i)^(1-n(i,j))(Y_j)=0; the minus signs in the exponents and p.508 opposition formula are present in the PDF although missing from pdftotext output.

proof.text: If $I=\varnothing$, its basis property gives $\mathfrak h^\vee=0$, hence $\mathfrak h=0$ and $R=\varnothing$. The assumed decomposition gives $\mathfrak g=0$. The free Lie algebra on no symbols is zero by its universal property: its identity and zero endomorphisms agree on every generator and hence agree. Its quotient is zero too, and the asserted map is the unique isomorphism $0\to0$. Henceforth suppose $I\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, pp.503--504; empty-base case supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Put $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak h$. Jacobi gives $[\mathfrak g_\beta,\mathfrak g_\gamma]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\beta+\gamma}$: for $x,y$ of weights $\beta,\gamma$, $[t,[x,y]]=(\beta(t)+\gamma(t))[x,y]$. A weight not in $R\cup\{0\}$ has zero space by the given decomposition. For $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$, $(\operatorname{ad}x)^n\mathfrak g_\beta$ therefore has weight $\beta+n\alpha$. These weights are distinct as $n$ varies, so all sufficiently large powers vanish, since $R\cup\{0\}$ is finite. The same holds for any vector by its finite weight expansion. Thus every root-vector adjoint is locally nilpotent. For each $\alpha$, one-dimensionality of the opposite root spaces makes their bracket span at most one-dimensional; it contains $h_\alpha\ne0$. Choosing nonzero vectors and rescaling one gives $x_\alpha,y_\alpha$ with $[x_\alpha,y_\alpha]=h_\alpha$. The weight equations and $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$ give the normalized sl2 relations.

source.place: Section 23h, p.503 root decomposition and p.508 normalized triples; direct Jacobi and finite-weight calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-integrable-sl2-reflection-automorphism] to each triple from step 2 with $\mathfrak t=\mathfrak h$. It gives an automorphism carrying weight $\beta$ to $\beta-\beta(h_\alpha)\alpha$. Thus $T_\alpha(\beta)=\beta-\beta(h_\alpha)\alpha$ permutes $R$: it is a linear involution, and it sends no root to $0$, since the injective map carries $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak h$ onto $\mathfrak g_0$ and so cannot also carry a nonzero $\mathfrak g_\beta$, $\beta\ne0$, into it. These are exactly the intrinsic reflections of the assumed root system, as follows directly. The group generated by all $T_\alpha$ and all intrinsic root reflections embeds in the permutation group of $R$, because $R$ spans $V=\mathfrak h^\vee$; it is finite. Average a rational coordinate dot product over this group to get a positive definite invariant rational form $B$. For any reflection $v\mapsto v-c(v)\alpha$ in this group with $c(\alpha)=2$, its fixed hyperplane is orthogonal to its negative eigenspace $\mathbf Q\alpha$, so $c(v)=2B(v,\alpha)/B(\alpha,\alpha)$. This formula identifies both reflections attached to $\alpha$. In particular the intrinsic coroot functional $c_\alpha$ is evaluation at $h_\alpha$, and all its values on roots are integral by crystallographicity.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, pp.503--504; Appendix C.19--C.20, p.611, invariant-form coroot formula; explicit comparison supplied by Q19.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-serre-rational-presentation] with $V=\mathfrak h^\vee$, the given $R$, the coroot functionals of step 3, and the prescribed base. The hypotheses hold: $R$ is finite, reduced and spanning; the coroots have value $2$, preserve $R$ by reflection, and have integral pairings. Its matrix is precisely $a_{ij}=\alpha_j(h_{\alpha_i})$, so its quotient is the $\mathfrak s(A)$ in the item. The cited theorem identifies the span of $H_i$ with $V^\vee$ by $H_i\mapsto c_{\alpha_i}$. In particular $h_{\alpha_i}$ form a basis of $\mathfrak h$ under the finite-dimensional evaluation identification $\mathfrak h\simeq V^\vee$. It also gives $\dim\mathfrak s(A)=|I|+|R|$: the $H_i$ span a diagonal maximal abelian subalgebra, its zero-weight space equals that subalgebra (a vector centralizing it could otherwise enlarge it to an abelian subalgebra), and every nonzero root space has dimension one.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, pp.503--504 and characteristic-zero extension p.508.

proof.text: For $i\ne j$, $\alpha_i-\alpha_j$ has mixed-sign simple-root coordinates, so is neither zero nor a root. Step 2 gives $[e_i,f_j]=[f_i,e_j]=0$. The Cartan relations follow from the weight equations and abelianness of $\mathfrak h$; $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$ is assumed. Here $a_{ii}=\alpha_i(h_{\alpha_i})=2$, and $a_{ij}\in\mathbf Z$ by step 3. For $i\ne j$, step 3 makes $T_{\alpha_i}(\alpha_j)=\alpha_j-a_{ij}\alpha_i$ a root; its $\alpha_j$-coordinate is $1>0$, so the sign condition on the base forces its $\alpha_i$-coordinate $-a_{ij}$ to be $\ge0$. This proves the asserted $a_{ij}\le0$. Put $n=-a_{ij}\ge0$. In the finite-dimensional adjoint representation of $\mathfrak g$, $e_j$ is a primitive vector of weight $n$ for the triple $(-h_{\alpha_i},f_i,e_i)$: its raising operator kills it and $[-h_{\alpha_i},e_j]=ne_j$. The swapped triple satisfies the required bracket relations by antisymmetry. Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-primitive-string-vanishing] to get $(\operatorname{ad}e_i)^{n+1}e_j=0$. Apply it again to $f_j$ for the original triple $(h_{\alpha_i},e_i,f_i)$ to obtain $(\operatorname{ad}f_i)^{n+1}f_j=0$. Both vectors and both triple Cartan elements are nonzero by the hypotheses. Thus every defining relation vanishes. The free universal map kills the ideal they generate, since its kernel is an ideal, and factors through the quotient to a Lie homomorphism $\phi$ with the prescribed generator values.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, p.504 relations and p.508 pinning; primitive-string lemma in Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/Sl2.lean:217--226.

proof.text: Every root is in the orbit of a positive or negative simple root under simple reflections. Here is the height argument needed for that assertion. For a positive root $\beta=\sum m_i\alpha_i$, positivity gives $0<B(\beta,\beta)=\sum m_iB(\beta,\alpha_i)$, so some $i$ with $m_i>0$ has $c_{\alpha_i}(\beta)>0$. This is a positive integer. Its reflection changes only the $i$-coefficient and strictly decreases the height $\sum m_i$. If another coefficient is positive, the reflected root cannot be negative by the sign condition; hence it is positive and induction applies. If no other coefficient is positive, reducedness forces $\beta=\alpha_i$. Induction on positive integer height terminates at a simple root. Apply the same argument to $-\beta$ for a negative root. This proves the assertion without irreducibility or a classification of root systems.

source.place: Appendix C.19--C.22, pp.611--612; explicit root-height descent using the invariant form of step 3.

proof.text: Let $U=\operatorname{im}\phi$. It contains every $e_i,f_i$ and, by step 4, all of $\mathfrak h$. Since $U$ is a subalgebra, it is stable under $\operatorname{ad}e_i,\operatorname{ad}f_i$ and all their powers, hence under their finite exponentials and their inverses. Consequently each reflection automorphism $w_i$ of [lem-sfb-integrable-sl2-reflection-automorphism] preserves $U$ in both directions. Its restriction maps $\mathfrak g_\beta$ isomorphically to $\mathfrak g_{s_i\beta}$. The one-dimensional simple and negative-simple root spaces already lie in $U$ because their chosen vectors are nonzero. Step 6 now propagates this to every root space. The given decomposition proves $U=\mathfrak g$, so $\phi$ is surjective. The same decomposition gives $\dim\mathfrak g=|I|+|R|$, equal to the dimension of $\mathfrak s(A)$ from [lem-sfb-serre-rational-presentation]. Rank-nullity makes $\phi$ injective. Its linear inverse preserves brackets by applying $\phi$ and using injectivity, so $\phi$ is the asserted rational Lie isomorphism.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, pp.503--504 and p.508; prescribed-pinning comparison assembled explicitly by Q19.
